fields.Question: Implement a thread-safe bounded blocking queue with put() and get(). put blocks when the queue is full, get blocks when it is empty. Do not use queue.Queue.
fields.Answer:
Key insight: protect the buffer with one mutex and use two condition variables, one producers wait on (not_full) and one consumers wait on (not_empty). Always re-check the predicate in a while loop after waking.

import threading
from collections import deque

class BoundedQueue:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.items = deque()
        lock = threading.Lock()
        self.not_full = threading.Condition(lock)
        self.not_empty = threading.Condition(lock)

    def put(self, item):
        with self.not_full:
            while len(self.items) >= self.capacity:
                self.not_full.wait()
            self.items.append(item)
            self.not_empty.notify()

    def get(self):
        with self.not_empty:
            while not self.items:
                self.not_empty.wait()
            item = self.items.popleft()
            self.not_full.notify()
            return item

Complexity: O(1) per operation, O(capacity) space.

Pitfalls: using if instead of while (spurious wakeups, or another consumer stealing the item); a single condition with notify() can wake the wrong kind of waiter and stall; notifying outside the lock is legal but the state change itself must happen under the lock.

Follow-ups: add timeouts (wait returns False on timeout, so loop with a deadline), add close() that wakes everyone with notify_all and makes get raise, or make it lock-free with a ring buffer for single producer single consumer.
fields.Hint: Producer consumer: one lock, two condition variables, wait in a while loop.
fields.Fact: Bounded buffer = mutex + not_full + not_empty, and every wait sits inside while(predicate).

fields.Question: Solve the bounded-buffer producer consumer problem using only semaphores. Explain why the order of acquire calls matters.
fields.Answer:
Approach: empty starts at N (free slots), full starts at 0 (filled slots), and a mutex guards the buffer indices.

import threading

class SemaphoreBuffer:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.buf = [None] * n
        self.n = n
        self.head = self.tail = 0
        self.empty = threading.Semaphore(n)
        self.full = threading.Semaphore(0)
        self.mutex = threading.Lock()

    def put(self, item):
        self.empty.acquire()
        with self.mutex:
            self.buf[self.tail] = item
            self.tail = (self.tail + 1) % self.n
        self.full.release()

    def get(self):
        self.full.acquire()
        with self.mutex:
            item = self.buf[self.head]
            self.head = (self.head + 1) % self.n
        self.empty.release()
        return item

Why order matters: if put takes the mutex first and then blocks on empty while the buffer is full, it sleeps holding the mutex. No consumer can enter to free a slot, so everyone deadlocks. Always wait on the counting semaphore first, then take the mutex only around the buffer access.

Tradeoff vs condition variables: semaphores encode the count for you, which is neat for this problem, but conditions generalise better to arbitrary predicates (for example wait until at least k items).
fields.Hint: Two counting semaphores track slots, one mutex protects the buffer.
fields.Fact: Acquire the counting semaphore before the mutex, never while holding it.

fields.Question: You have N producer threads and M consumer threads sharing a queue. How do you shut the system down cleanly so every queued item is processed and every thread exits?
fields.Answer:
1. Join all producers so no new work arrives.
  2. Put one sentinel (poison pill) per consumer into the queue. FIFO order guarantees real items ahead of the pills are processed first.
  3. Each consumer exits its loop when it receives the sentinel.
  4. Join the consumers.
import queue, threading

STOP = object()

def consumer(q, handle):
    while True:
        item = q.get()
        try:
            if item is STOP:
                return
            handle(item)
        finally:
            q.task_done()

def shutdown(q, producers, consumers):
    for t in producers:
        t.join()
    for _ in consumers:
        q.put(STOP)
    for t in consumers:
        t.join()

Alternatives: q.join() blocks until every put has a matching task_done, useful when consumers are long lived daemons. Python 3.13 adds Queue.shutdown(). A shared Event flag works only if consumers use get(timeout=...) so they can notice it.

Pitfalls: one pill for many consumers leaves the others blocked forever; an exception inside handle that skips task_done makes q.join hang; daemon threads killed at exit can lose in-flight work.
fields.Hint: Poison pills, one per consumer, after producers finish.
fields.Fact: Sentinel count must equal consumer count, and sentinels go in after producers stop.

fields.Question: Implement a counting semaphore using only a mutex and a condition variable.
fields.Answer:
import threading

class Semaphore:
    def __init__(self, value=1):
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("value must be >= 0")
        self.value = value
        self.cond = threading.Condition(threading.Lock())

    def acquire(self):
        with self.cond:
            while self.value == 0:
                self.cond.wait()
            self.value -= 1

    def release(self):
        with self.cond:
            self.value += 1
            self.cond.notify()

Why it is correct: the count only changes under the lock, and acquire re-checks the predicate after every wakeup, so two threads cannot both take the last permit.

Follow-ups: acquire(timeout) with a deadline loop; a bounded semaphore that raises if release would exceed the initial value (catches double release bugs); fairness, since condition wakeups are not FIFO and a waiter can starve.

Complexity: O(1) per call, ignoring time spent blocked.

fields.Fact: Semaphore = counter + mutex + condition; the predicate is value > 0.

fields.Question: Implement a readers-writer lock: many readers may hold it at once, a writer needs exclusive access. Make sure writers cannot starve.
fields.Answer:
import threading

class RWLock:
    def __init__(self):
        self.cond = threading.Condition()
        self.readers = 0
        self.writer = False
        self.waiting_writers = 0

    def acquire_read(self):
        with self.cond:
            while self.writer or self.waiting_writers:
                self.cond.wait()
            self.readers += 1

    def release_read(self):
        with self.cond:
            self.readers -= 1
            if self.readers == 0:
                self.cond.notify_all()

    def acquire_write(self):
        with self.cond:
            self.waiting_writers += 1
            while self.writer or self.readers:
                self.cond.wait()
            self.waiting_writers -= 1
            self.writer = True

    def release_write(self):
        with self.cond:
            self.writer = False
            self.cond.notify_all()

Key insight: the naive version (readers enter whenever no writer is active) starves writers under a steady stream of readers. Blocking new readers while a writer waits gives writer preference.

Tradeoffs: writer preference can starve readers if writes are constant; fair (FIFO ticket) locks fix both but cost more. RW locks only pay off when critical sections are long and reads dominate; for short sections a plain mutex is often faster because the RW lock's own bookkeeping is a contended write.

Pitfalls: upgrading a read lock to a write lock deadlocks if two readers try at once; recursive read acquisition can deadlock with writer preference.
fields.Hint: Track active readers, active writer and waiting writers; readers yield to waiting writers.
fields.Fact: Writer preference: new readers wait if any writer is waiting.

fields.Question: Two threads share a counter. One prints odd numbers, the other even numbers, and together they must print 1 to N in order. Write it.
fields.Answer:
import threading

def print_alternating(n):
    cond = threading.Condition()
    state = {"next": 1}

    def worker(parity):
        while True:
            with cond:
                while state["next"] <= n and state["next"] % 2 != parity:
                    cond.wait()
                if state["next"] > n:
                    cond.notify_all()
                    return
                print(state["next"])
                state["next"] += 1
                cond.notify_all()

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(p,)) for p in (1, 0)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

Key insight: the condition predicate is "is it my turn or are we done". The termination check must be part of the wait predicate, otherwise the last thread sleeps forever.

Alternatives: two semaphores handing a token back and forth (odd releases even, even releases odd) is shorter and generalises to k threads in a ring.

Pitfalls: busy-waiting on a shared variable without synchronisation; forgetting notify_all on exit.
fields.Hint: Shared turn state plus a condition variable.
fields.Fact: Turn-taking = predicate on shared state, checked under a lock, including the exit condition.

fields.Question: Three methods first(), second(), third() are called from three different threads in arbitrary order. Guarantee they always run in the order first, second, third. (LeetCode 1114)
fields.Answer:
import threading

class Foo:
    def __init__(self):
        self.first_done = threading.Event()
        self.second_done = threading.Event()

    def first(self, print_first):
        print_first()
        self.first_done.set()

    def second(self, print_second):
        self.first_done.wait()
        print_second()
        self.second_done.set()

    def third(self, print_third):
        self.second_done.wait()
        print_third()

Key insight: you need happens-before edges, not mutual exclusion. An Event (or a semaphore initialised to 0, or a latch) expresses "wait until X has happened" and is safe even if the signal fires before anyone waits, because the state is remembered.

Pitfalls: using a condition variable without a flag loses the signal if notify happens before wait; spinning on a boolean wastes CPU and, in languages like Java or C++, is a data race without volatile or atomics.

fields.Fact: Ordering between threads needs a remembered signal (event, semaphore at 0, latch), not a lock.

fields.Question: Implement a reusable barrier for N threads: each call to wait() blocks until all N threads have arrived, then all proceed, and the barrier can be used again for the next round.
fields.Answer:
import threading

class Barrier:
    def __init__(self, parties):
        self.parties = parties
        self.count = 0
        self.generation = 0
        self.cond = threading.Condition()

    def wait(self):
        with self.cond:
            gen = self.generation
            self.count += 1
            if self.count == self.parties:
                self.generation += 1
                self.count = 0
                self.cond.notify_all()
                return
            while gen == self.generation:
                self.cond.wait()

Key insight: waiting on count == parties breaks on reuse, because the last thread resets count before the others wake and they go back to sleep. Waiting on a generation change is robust: once it bumps, it never matches the captured value again.

Follow-ups: what if a thread dies before arriving? Production barriers (threading.Barrier, Java CyclicBarrier) support timeouts and a broken state that wakes everyone with an error.
fields.Hint: Count arrivals, use a generation number so late wakers do not get confused by the next round.
fields.Fact: Reusable barrier: wait on a generation counter, not on the arrival count.

fields.Question: Build a fixed-size thread pool from scratch: submit(fn, *args) returns a future-like object whose result() blocks until the task finishes and re-raises its exception.
fields.Answer:
import queue, threading

class Future:
    def __init__(self):
        self._done = threading.Event()
        self._result = self._error = None

    def set(self, result=None, error=None):
        self._result, self._error = result, error
        self._done.set()

    def result(self, timeout=None):
        if not self._done.wait(timeout):
            raise TimeoutError
        if self._error:
            raise self._error
        return self._result

class ThreadPool:
    def __init__(self, workers):
        self.tasks = queue.Queue()
        self.threads = [threading.Thread(target=self._run) for _ in range(workers)]
        for t in self.threads:
            t.start()

    def submit(self, fn, *args):
        fut = Future()
        self.tasks.put((fn, args, fut))
        return fut

    def _run(self):
        while (task := self.tasks.get()) is not None:
            fn, args, fut = task
            try:
                fut.set(result=fn(*args))
            except BaseException as e:
                fut.set(error=e)

    def shutdown(self):
        for _ in self.threads:
            self.tasks.put(None)
        for t in self.threads:
            t.join()

Points to raise: catch exceptions per task so one failure does not kill a worker; an unbounded queue hides overload, so production pools bound it and pick a rejection policy (block, drop, caller runs); a task that submits to the same pool and waits on the result can deadlock once all workers are blocked doing the same.

Sizing: about the number of cores for CPU-bound work, more for I/O-bound work.
fields.Hint: Worker threads pulling from a shared queue; the future is an Event plus a slot.
fields.Fact: Thread pool = bounded work queue + N workers + futures; isolate task failures.

fields.Question: Five philosophers sit at a round table with one fork between each pair. Each needs both neighbouring forks to eat. Write a solution that cannot deadlock.
fields.Answer:
Why naive code deadlocks: if everyone picks up the left fork first, all five can hold one fork and wait forever for the right one. That satisfies all four Coffman conditions, including circular wait.

import threading

forks = [threading.Lock() for _ in range(5)]

def dine(i, eat):
    left, right = i, (i + 1) % 5
    first, second = sorted((left, right))
    with forks[first]:
        with forks[second]:
            eat(i)

Key insight: always acquiring the lower numbered fork first imposes a total order on locks, so a cycle in the waits-for graph is impossible.

Other fixes: a semaphore that lets at most four philosophers try at once; try-lock the second fork and back off (risks livelock without random backoff); a waiter/arbiter that hands out both forks atomically.

Follow-up: ordering prevents deadlock but not starvation; a philosopher can keep losing the race unless locks are fair.
fields.Hint: Break circular wait with a global lock order.
fields.Fact: Global lock ordering removes circular wait, the cheapest Coffman condition to break.

fields.Question: Implement a thread-safe token bucket rate limiter: allow(), returns True if a request may proceed, with rate r tokens per second and burst capacity b.
fields.Answer:
import threading, time

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate, capacity):
        self.rate = rate
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.tokens = capacity
        self.updated = time.monotonic()
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def allow(self, cost=1):
        with self.lock:
            now = time.monotonic()
            elapsed = now - self.updated
            self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + elapsed * self.rate)
            self.updated = now
            if self.tokens >= cost:
                self.tokens -= cost
                return True
            return False

Key insight: compute the refill on demand from the elapsed time instead of a timer thread, so each call is O(1) and the state is two numbers.

Pitfalls: time.time() can jump backwards with clock adjustments, use a monotonic clock; reading and updating tokens outside the lock lets two threads spend the same token; a single global lock becomes the bottleneck at very high QPS, so shard per key or per core.

Follow-ups: blocking acquire (sleep for (cost - tokens) / rate), per-user buckets in a dict with eviction, distributed version in Redis with an atomic script.
fields.Hint: Refill lazily from elapsed time; no background thread.
fields.Fact: Token bucket refills lazily from a monotonic clock under one lock.

fields.Question: You need to fetch 10,000 URLs with asyncio but the remote API allows at most 20 concurrent requests. Write the core of it.
fields.Answer:
import asyncio

async def fetch_all(urls, fetch, limit=20):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(limit)

    async def one(url):
        async with sem:
            return await fetch(url)

    return await asyncio.gather(*(one(u) for u in urls), return_exceptions=True)

Key insight: the semaphore bounds in-flight requests, not tasks; all coroutines exist but only 20 are past the async with at once.

Tradeoffs: creating 10,000 task objects is cheap for asyncio, but for millions use a fixed set of 20 worker coroutines pulling from an asyncio.Queue so memory stays O(limit). return_exceptions=True keeps one failure from cancelling the rest; asyncio.TaskGroup (3.11+) gives structured cancellation if you want fail-fast instead.

Pitfalls: calling a blocking HTTP library inside the coroutine serialises everything on the event loop; forgetting timeouts lets a few slow hosts hold all 20 permits; retries need backoff with jitter.
fields.Hint: asyncio.Semaphore around the request; gather the tasks.
fields.Fact: Bound concurrency with a semaphore or a fixed worker pool, never by hoping the server copes.

fields.Question: Implement a CountDownLatch: initialised with n, count_down() decrements it, and await_zero() blocks until the count reaches zero. Where would you use it?
fields.Answer:
import threading

class CountDownLatch:
    def __init__(self, count):
        self.count = count
        self.cond = threading.Condition()

    def count_down(self):
        with self.cond:
            if self.count > 0:
                self.count -= 1
                if self.count == 0:
                    self.cond.notify_all()

    def await_zero(self, timeout=None):
        with self.cond:
            return self.cond.wait_for(lambda: self.count == 0, timeout)

Uses: main thread waits for N workers to finish initialisation, or tests start N threads and release them together (latch of 1 as a start gun).

Versus a barrier: a latch is one-shot and the waiters are not the ones counting down; a barrier is reusable and every party both arrives and waits.

Note: wait_for re-checks the predicate in a loop internally, which is the while-loop rule packaged up.
fields.Hint: Counter + condition; notify_all when it hits zero.
fields.Fact: Latch: one-shot, someone else counts down; barrier: reusable, everyone arrives.

fields.Question: Design and implement a timer scheduler: schedule(delay, fn) runs fn after delay seconds on a single background thread. New tasks can be scheduled while it is sleeping, including ones due sooner than the current earliest.
fields.Answer:
import heapq, itertools, threading, time

class Scheduler:
    def __init__(self):
        self.heap = []
        self.seq = itertools.count()
        self.cond = threading.Condition()
        threading.Thread(target=self._run, daemon=True).start()

    def schedule(self, delay, fn):
        with self.cond:
            due = time.monotonic() + delay
            heapq.heappush(self.heap, (due, next(self.seq), fn))
            self.cond.notify()

    def _run(self):
        while True:
            with self.cond:
                while not self.heap:
                    self.cond.wait()
                due, _, fn = self.heap[0]
                wait = due - time.monotonic()
                if wait > 0:
                    self.cond.wait(wait)
                    continue
                heapq.heappop(self.heap)
            fn()

Key insight: sleep on the condition with a timeout until the earliest deadline, and have schedule() notify so the worker re-evaluates when an earlier task arrives. After any wakeup, recompute rather than assume.

Complexity: O(log n) schedule and pop, O(n) space.

Pitfalls: running fn while holding the lock blocks schedule() and can deadlock if fn schedules; the sequence number breaks ties so functions are never compared; use a monotonic clock. Follow-ups: cancellation (mark entries cancelled, lazy deletion), running callbacks on a pool so a slow task does not delay the others.

fields.Fact: Timer queue = heap of deadlines + condition.wait(timeout) + notify on insert.

fields.Question: Building H2O (LeetCode 1117): hydrogen and oxygen threads arrive in any order. Release them in groups of exactly two H and one O so each group forms a molecule before the next group starts.
fields.Answer:
import threading

class H2O:
    def __init__(self):
        self.h_slots = threading.Semaphore(2)
        self.o_slots = threading.Semaphore(1)
        self.barrier = threading.Barrier(3)

    def hydrogen(self, release_hydrogen):
        with self.h_slots:
            self.barrier.wait()
            release_hydrogen()

    def oxygen(self, release_oxygen):
        with self.o_slots:
            self.barrier.wait()
            release_oxygen()

Key insight: split the problem into admission (at most 2 H and 1 O in the current group) and rendezvous (all three present). The semaphores cap who enters, the barrier makes the three wait for each other.

Subtle point: each thread releases its slot only after passing the barrier and bonding, so the next group cannot start filling until the current one leaves the barrier.

Pattern: this admission plus rendezvous structure reappears in many group-forming problems (party of k, ride sharing with mixed types).

fields.Question: Count word frequencies across 64 large text files as fast as possible on an 8-core machine in Python. Sketch the code and explain the design.
fields.Answer:
from collections import Counter
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def count_file(path):
    counts = Counter()
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            counts.update(line.split())
    return counts

def word_counts(paths):
    total = Counter()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
        for partial in pool.map(count_file, paths, chunksize=4):
            total.update(partial)
    return total

Why processes: tokenising and counting is CPU-bound, and the GIL stops threads from running Python bytecode in parallel. Each process has its own interpreter.

Design points: send paths to workers, not file contents, to avoid pickling large data; each worker streams its file line by line so memory stays bounded; reduce by merging counters. chunksize cuts IPC overhead for many small tasks.

Tradeoffs: if the files live on one slow disk, you are I/O-bound and more processes will not help; if the vocabulary is huge, returning full counters is expensive, so pre-aggregate top-k per worker or hash-partition words to reducers.

fields.Fact: Map-reduce with processes for CPU-bound Python; move small messages, not big data.

fields.Question: Ten threads each run counter += 1 a million times on a shared global. The final value is often less than 10 million. Explain exactly why and fix it. Does the GIL save you?
fields.Answer:
Why: counter += 1 is three steps: load the value, add one, store it. Two threads can both load 41, both compute 42 and both store 42, so one increment is lost. In CPython the GIL can switch threads between those bytecodes, so the GIL makes individual bytecodes safe, not your read-modify-write sequence.

import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def work(n):
    global counter
    for _ in range(n):
        with lock:
            counter += 1

Better designs: have each thread count locally and add once at the end (one lock acquisition per thread instead of per increment), or use a language atomic (AtomicLong, std::atomic fetch_add).

Follow-ups: free-threaded CPython (3.13t) removes the GIL, which makes such bugs show up more often, not less. In C or Java this is also a data race with undefined or weakly defined visibility, not just a lost update.

fields.Fact: Lost update: any read-modify-write on shared data needs a lock or an atomic, GIL or not.

fields.Question: Find the bug: a cache does `if key not in cache: cache[key] = expensive(key)` from many threads. What can go wrong and how do you fix it without serialising all computations?
fields.Answer:
Bug: check-then-act is not atomic. Several threads can see the key missing at the same time and all call expensive(key). Results may be correct but you do the work N times (a cache stampede), and if expensive has side effects you get duplicates.

Naive fix: one lock around the whole thing, which serialises every cache miss, even for different keys.

Better: store a future per key under a short lock, compute outside the lock, and have everyone else wait on the same future.
import threading
from concurrent.futures import Future

class OnceCache:
    def __init__(self, compute):
        self.compute = compute
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.futures = {}

    def get(self, key):
        with self.lock:
            fut = self.futures.get(key)
            owner = fut is None
            if owner:
                fut = self.futures[key] = Future()
        if owner:
            try:
                fut.set_result(self.compute(key))
            except BaseException as e:
                fut.set_exception(e)
                with self.lock:
                    del self.futures[key]
        return fut.result()

Points: never run the expensive call while holding the global lock; decide whether failures are cached (here they are evicted so a retry is possible); add TTLs and size bounds for real use.
fields.Hint: Check-then-act race, plus a thundering herd on the same key.
fields.Fact: Check-then-act must be atomic; dedupe in-flight work with a per-key future.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)
concurrent.futures, Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html)

fields.Question: Two threads run transfer(a, b, amount) and transfer(b, a, amount) at the same time. Each transfer locks the source account, then the destination. The service hangs. Explain and fix.
fields.Answer:
Diagnosis: thread 1 holds a and waits for b, thread 2 holds b and waits for a. All four Coffman conditions hold: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.

def transfer(src, dst, amount):
    first, second = sorted((src, dst), key=lambda acct: acct.id)
    with first.lock:
        with second.lock:
            if src.balance < amount:
                raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
            src.balance -= amount
            dst.balance += amount

Key insight: lock acquisition order must depend on a global, stable property (account id), not on the call's argument order. Then no cycle can form.

Edge cases: src is dst (with a non-reentrant lock, sorting gives the same lock twice and you self-deadlock; handle it explicitly); ids must be unique and immutable.

Alternatives: try-lock with timeout and back off (needs jitter to avoid livelock); a single lock for all accounts (simple, no parallelism); in a database, rely on its deadlock detector and retry the transaction.
fields.Hint: Deadlock from inconsistent lock order; order locks by a stable key.
fields.Fact: Acquire multiple locks in a global order by a stable id.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)
Linux kernel docs: Runtime locking correctness validator (https://docs.kernel.org/locking/lockdep-design.html)

fields.Question: Code review: a consumer does `with cond: if not queue: cond.wait()` then pops from the queue. It occasionally crashes with IndexError on pop. Why?
fields.Answer:
Why: waking up from wait does not mean the condition is true. Another consumer may have been woken too, or barged in and taken the item between the notify and this thread reacquiring the lock (Mesa semantics). POSIX and Python also permit spurious wakeups.

with cond:
    while not queue:
        cond.wait()
    item = queue.popleft()

Or: cond.wait_for(lambda: queue), which loops for you.

Related pitfalls: notify() when different waiters wait for different predicates can wake the wrong one, use notify_all or separate conditions; modifying the shared state without holding the condition's lock creates lost wakeups.
fields.Hint: Wait belongs in a while loop.
fields.Fact: Mesa semantics: always while (not predicate) wait().
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Condition Variables (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-cv.pdf)
pthread_cond_wait, The Open Group Base Specifications (https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_cond_wait.html)

fields.Question: A worker does `while not ready:` followed by `with cond: cond.wait()` inside the loop body. The setter does `with cond: ready = True; cond.notify()`. Rarely, the worker sleeps forever even though ready is True. Find the bug.
fields.Answer:
Interleaving: the worker reads ready (False) without the lock. Before it acquires cond, the setter takes the lock, sets ready and notifies. Nobody is waiting, so the notify is dropped. The worker then acquires the lock and waits for a notify that already happened.

Rule: read and write the predicate while holding the same lock the condition uses, and check it inside the locked region. Then check-and-sleep is atomic, because wait releases the lock and sleeps in one step.

def set_ready():
    global ready
    with cond:
        ready = True
        cond.notify_all()

def wait_ready():
    with cond:
        while not ready:
            cond.wait()

Alternative: threading.Event already packages a flag plus condition correctly.

Takeaway: a condition variable is stateless; the shared state is what remembers the signal, so it must be protected and checked under the lock.
fields.Hint: Lost wakeup: the predicate check is not under the lock.
fields.Fact: Condition variables do not remember notifies; the guarded state does, so check and mutate it under the lock.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Condition Variables (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-cv.pdf)
pthread_cond_wait, The Open Group Base Specifications (https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_cond_wait.html)
threading, Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html)

fields.Question: An event bus holds a lock while it iterates subscribers and calls each callback. Occasionally the whole app freezes. What is likely happening and how do you redesign it?
fields.Answer:
Likely cause: a callback calls back into the bus (subscribe, publish) and tries to take the same non-reentrant lock, self-deadlock; or a callback takes another lock that some other thread holds while waiting on the bus lock, a lock-order cycle; or it just blocks on I/O and stalls every publisher.

Fix: copy the subscriber list under the lock, release it, then invoke callbacks.

def publish(self, event):
    with self.lock:
        subscribers = list(self.subscribers)
    for callback in subscribers:
        callback(event)

Tradeoffs: a subscriber removed concurrently may receive one more event, which is usually acceptable and should be documented. An RLock hides the self-deadlock case but not the cross-lock cycle, and reentrancy means the list can change under your iteration.

Principle: keep critical sections small and closed: no callbacks, no I/O, no waiting on other locks inside them.
fields.Hint: Never call unknown code while holding a lock.
fields.Fact: Snapshot under the lock, call out after releasing it.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: A production Python or JVM service is hung: CPU is near zero and requests time out. Walk through how you confirm a deadlock and find the cause.
fields.Answer:
1. Confirm it is blocked, not busy: low CPU, threads in sleeping state (top -H, /proc/PID/task/*/stat).
  2. Dump all thread stacks without killing the process: py-spy dump --pid PID for Python, jstack or kill -3 for the JVM (it also reports detected Java-level deadlocks), gdb with thread apply all bt for native code.
  3. Look for threads blocked in lock acquire, and work out which lock each holds and which it wants. A cycle is a deadlock; a long chain behind one thread stuck on I/O is a stall, not a deadlock.
  4. Check for external waits: connection pool exhausted, a thread waiting on a future that will never be completed because the pool that would complete it is full.

Fix and prevent: impose lock ordering, add timeouts to lock and pool acquires so hangs turn into errors with stacks, use lock-order checkers in tests (lockdep in the kernel, ThreadSanitizer for C/C++, Go's race detector for data races).

Pitfall: restarting fixes the symptom and destroys the evidence; capture dumps first.
fields.Hint: Dump every thread's stack and look for a cycle of lock waits.
fields.Fact: Thread dumps first, then find the cycle; add timeouts so future hangs report themselves.
fields.Source:
py-spy: Sampling profiler for Python programs (https://github.com/benfred/py-spy)
Linux kernel docs: Runtime locking correctness validator (https://docs.kernel.org/locking/lockdep-design.html)
OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)

fields.Question: Two threads keep trying to acquire two locks with try-lock, and on failure each releases what it has and retries immediately. The system is not deadlocked, CPU is at 100 percent, and no work completes. What is this and how do you fix it?
fields.Answer:
Diagnosis: livelock. Threads are active but keep undoing each other in lockstep, so no progress is made. Unlike deadlock, state changes constantly, and stack dumps show threads moving.

Fixes: randomised exponential backoff before retrying, so attempts desynchronise; better, remove the need for try-lock by using a global lock order; or have a single arbiter decide.

import random, time

def acquire_both(a, b, max_backoff=0.1):
    delay = 0.001
    while True:
        with a:
            if b.acquire(blocking=False):
                return
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0, delay))
        delay = min(delay * 2, max_backoff)

Related: starvation is when one thread never gets the resource while others do, often from unfair locks or priority scheduling; fix with fair (FIFO) locks or aging. The same jittered backoff idea is why network clients retry with jitter.
fields.Hint: Livelock; break symmetry with randomised backoff.
fields.Fact: Livelock: active but no progress; jittered backoff breaks the symmetry.
fields.Source: OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)

fields.Question: A low-priority thread holds a mutex that a high-priority thread needs, and a medium-priority CPU-bound thread keeps running. The high-priority thread misses its deadline. What is this, and how do real systems fix it?
fields.Answer:
Diagnosis: priority inversion. The high-priority thread waits on the low one, but the scheduler prefers the medium thread over the low one, so the lock holder never runs and the high thread is effectively blocked by the medium one. Mars Pathfinder hit exactly this in 1997 and kept resetting until the mutex was switched to priority inheritance.

Fixes:

  • Priority inheritance: the lock holder temporarily runs at the highest priority of its waiters (PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT, Linux rt-mutexes).
  • Priority ceiling: the lock has a fixed high priority that any holder runs at.
  • Design: keep critical sections short and avoid sharing locks across priority classes.

When it matters: real-time and embedded systems, audio threads, and any app that mixes priority levels (iOS QoS classes surface this as priority inversion warnings).
fields.Hint: Priority inversion; priority inheritance.
fields.Fact: Priority inversion is fixed by priority inheritance on the lock.
fields.Source:
What really happened on Mars? (Glenn Reeves account) (https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs614/1999sp/papers/pathfinder.html)
Linux kernel docs: RT-mutex subsystem with PI support (https://docs.kernel.org/locking/rt-mutex.html)

fields.Question: One thread iterates over a shared dict to build a report while other threads insert into it. Sometimes it raises "dictionary changed size during iteration", and in other languages it may silently corrupt or crash. How do you fix it, and what are the tradeoffs of each option?
fields.Answer:
• Lock the whole iteration: correct and simple, but writers stall for the length of the report.
  • Snapshot under the lock: copy = dict(shared) under the lock, iterate the copy without it. Short critical section, costs O(n) memory and time per snapshot, and the report reflects one consistent moment.
  • Copy-on-write: writers build a new dict and swap a reference; readers grab the current reference and iterate an immutable object. Reads are lock-free, writes cost O(n), great for read-mostly config or routing tables.
  • Concurrent collections: ConcurrentHashMap in Java iterates weakly consistently without throwing, but the report may mix old and new entries.
with lock:
    snapshot = dict(shared)
report = build_report(snapshot)

Pitfall: a shallow snapshot shares mutable values, so if values are mutated in place you still have a race on them.
fields.Hint: Snapshot, lock for the full iteration, or immutable copy-on-write.
fields.Fact: Iterate a snapshot or an immutable version; keep the lock window to the copy.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: An asyncio web service has p99 latency of several seconds even though CPU is low. You find a handler that calls requests.get() and another that does time.sleep(1). Explain the problem and the fix.
fields.Answer:
Why: asyncio runs all coroutines on one thread. A blocking call never yields to the loop, so every other request waits until it returns. One slow call becomes everyone's latency.

Fixes:

  • Use async equivalents: await asyncio.sleep, an async HTTP client (aiohttp, httpx.AsyncClient), async DB drivers.
  • For unavoidable blocking or CPU work, offload: await asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...) or loop.run_in_executor with a process pool for CPU-bound work.

import asyncio

async def handler(path):
    data = await asyncio.to_thread(read_large_file, path)
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return data

Detecting it: run with PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 or loop.set_debug(True), which logs callbacks that take longer than loop.slow_callback_duration (100 ms default); sample stacks with py-spy.

Pitfall: to_thread uses a bounded default executor, so thousands of offloaded calls queue up; size it or use a proper async library.
fields.Hint: Blocking calls stall the event loop for every coroutine.
fields.Fact: Never block the event loop; await async I/O or offload to an executor.
fields.Source:
Developing with asyncio, Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-dev.html)
Coroutines and Tasks (asyncio), Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html)

fields.Question: Code review: `if not os.path.exists(path): with open(path, 'w') as f: f.write(data)` is meant to create a file only if it does not exist, with several processes running it. What is wrong and what is the correct approach?
fields.Answer:
Bug: time-of-check to time-of-use. Between exists() and open(), another process can create the file, and 'w' then truncates and overwrites it. In privileged code an attacker can swap in a symlink and redirect the write.

Fix: make the check and the create a single atomic syscall with O_CREAT | O_EXCL, which fails with EEXIST if the file exists. Python's 'x' mode does this.

try:
    with open(path, "x") as f:
        f.write(data)
except FileExistsError:
    pass

General principle: do not ask then act; attempt the operation and handle the error (EAFP). Same for mkdir, lock files, and rename-based claims.

Follow-ups: O_EXCL on NFS has historically been unreliable on old versions; for inter-process mutual exclusion prefer flock/fcntl locks or a database row lock; O_NOFOLLOW guards against symlink tricks.
fields.Hint: TOCTOU race; let the kernel do the check atomically.
fields.Fact: Check-then-use on files is a race; use O_CREAT|O_EXCL and handle EEXIST.
fields.Source:
open(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/open.2.html)
OSTEP: Interlude: Files and Directories (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/file-intro.pdf)

fields.Question: You are designing a service with many locks owned by different modules. How do you prevent deadlocks systematically rather than fixing them one at a time?
fields.Answer:
Framework: deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Break any one.

  • Circular wait (most practical): define a lock hierarchy or rank and always acquire in that order; enforce with a debug-mode checker that asserts the rank increases (the idea behind Linux lockdep).
  • Hold and wait: acquire everything you need up front, or never hold a lock while calling out or blocking.
  • No preemption: try-lock with timeout, release and retry, typical in databases which abort a victim transaction.
  • Mutual exclusion: avoid the lock: immutable data, message passing, single-writer ownership, or lock-free structures.

Operationally: timeouts on every lock and pool acquisition, thread dumps on timeout, and tests under ThreadSanitizer or stress with randomised scheduling.

Tradeoff: strict global ordering is hard across module boundaries; the most reliable designs reduce the number of locks any code path holds at once to one.
fields.Hint: Pick which Coffman condition you will break, and enforce it.
fields.Fact: Prevent deadlock by design: lock ordering, no calls out under locks, timeouts as a backstop.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)
Linux kernel docs: Runtime locking correctness validator (https://docs.kernel.org/locking/lockdep-design.html)

fields.Question: Mutex vs semaphore: when would you use each? Is a binary semaphore the same as a mutex?
fields.Answer:
• Mutex: mutual exclusion around a critical section. It has an owner: the thread that locked it must unlock it. That enables error checking, recursive variants and priority inheritance.
  • Counting semaphore: a permit counter. Use it to cap concurrency (at most 10 DB connections, 20 in-flight requests) or to count available items or slots.
  • Binary semaphore vs mutex: same counting behaviour, different semantics. A semaphore has no owner, so any thread may release it. That makes it a valid signalling tool (thread A releases, thread B was waiting), but you lose ownership checks and priority inheritance, and an accidental double release silently admits two threads.

Rule of thumb: protecting data, use a mutex; limiting how many or signalling that something happened, use a semaphore (or an event/latch for one-shot signals).

Follow-up: for protecting state while waiting on an arbitrary condition, neither is ideal; that is what condition variables are for.
fields.Hint: Ownership vs counting.
fields.Fact: Mutex = ownership for exclusion; semaphore = counter for capacity and signalling.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Semaphores (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-sema.pdf)
OSTEP: Locks (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-locks.pdf)
Linux kernel docs: RT-mutex subsystem with PI support (https://docs.kernel.org/locking/rt-mutex.html)

fields.Question: When do you reach for a condition variable instead of a semaphore or just polling a flag?
fields.Answer:
Use a condition variable when a thread must wait until some predicate over lock-protected state becomes true: queue non-empty, at least k items, my turn, all workers idle. The condition lets you sleep atomically while releasing the lock, and re-check on wakeup.

  • Semaphore fits when the predicate is simply "count > 0".
  • Polling a flag with sleep wastes CPU or adds latency, and without proper atomics it is a data race in C, C++ and Java.
  • Event / future fits one-shot "has X happened".

Usage rules: always paired with a mutex; always while (!predicate) wait(); modify the predicate state while holding the mutex; notify_all when waiters wait on different predicates or when a state change can satisfy several.

Pitfall: thundering herd from notify_all on a big pool; separate conditions per predicate (not_full, not_empty) reduce useless wakeups.
fields.Hint: Waiting for an arbitrary predicate over shared state.
fields.Fact: Condition variable: sleep until a predicate on locked state is true.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Condition Variables (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-cv.pdf)
pthread_cond_wait, The Open Group Base Specifications (https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_cond_wait.html)

fields.Question: Spinlock vs blocking mutex: when is spinning the right choice, and when is it a disaster?
fields.Answer:
• Spin when: critical sections are a few hundred nanoseconds, there are multiple cores, and the lock holder cannot be descheduled (kernel code with preemption disabled, interrupt handlers). Spinning avoids two context switches costing microseconds.
  • Disaster when: on a single core or when the holder gets preempted, spinners burn their entire time slice while the holder cannot run; under heavy contention spinners also hammer the cache line.

Real-world answer: most user-space mutexes are adaptive. glibc and Go spin briefly, then park the thread with a futex syscall. The uncontended path is a single atomic compare-and-swap with no syscall.

Follow-ups: test-and-test-and-set spinning reads the line locally before trying the atomic; ticket or MCS locks add fairness and reduce cache traffic; in user space you rarely should write your own spinlock.
fields.Hint: Spin only when the expected wait is shorter than a context switch and the holder is running.
fields.Fact: Spin briefly, then sleep; pure spinlocks belong in kernels and very short sections.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Locks (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-locks.pdf)
futex(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/futex.7.html)

fields.Question: Why is an uncontended mutex lock almost free, while a heavily contended one can cost tens of microseconds and destroy throughput?
fields.Answer:
Uncontended: lock is one atomic compare-and-swap on a word in user space, roughly tens of nanoseconds, no kernel involvement. Linux futexes are designed for this: the kernel is called only when the lock is already held.

Contended:

  • The waiter makes a futex syscall and sleeps; the releaser must make a syscall to wake it. That is two kernel transitions and two context switches.
  • The cache line holding the lock bounces between cores on every acquire.
  • Convoys form: threads queue behind the lock, and a holder that gets preempted stalls them all.

What to do: shrink critical sections, move work (allocation, I/O, logging) outside the lock, shard the lock (striping, per-core counters), use read-mostly structures, or batch so you take the lock once per N items.

How to see it: perf, off-CPU flame graphs, or lock profilers (Go mutex profile, JFR on the JVM) show time blocked on locks rather than on CPU.
fields.Hint: Futex fast path vs syscall, context switch and cache line bouncing.
fields.Fact: Locks are cheap; contention is expensive. Reduce contention, not lock count.
fields.Source:
futex(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/futex.7.html)
OSTEP: Locks (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-locks.pdf)
Flame Graphs (https://www.brendangregg.com/flamegraphs.html)

fields.Question: Implement a lock-free counter (or stack push) with compare-and-swap. What is the ABA problem and how is it avoided?
fields.Answer:
CAS loop: read the current value, compute the new one, and atomically swap only if the value is still what you read; otherwise retry. Python has no user-level CAS, so this is pseudocode in Python syntax, where cas(ref, expected, new) is assumed atomic:

def increment(counter):
    while True:
        old = counter.load()
        if counter.cas(old, old + 1):
            return old + 1

def push(stack, node):
    while True:
        node.next = stack.head.load()
        if stack.head.cas(node.next, node):
            return

ABA: in a lock-free stack pop, thread 1 reads head A and next B, gets paused; others pop A, pop B, push A back. Head is A again so thread 1's CAS succeeds and installs B, which was freed. The value matched but the state did not.

Fixes: tagged pointers or version counters swapped together (double-width CAS); safe memory reclamation such as hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation; in garbage-collected languages ABA from reuse mostly disappears because a node is not recycled while referenced.

Tradeoffs: lock-free is not automatically faster; under heavy contention CAS retries waste work. Use it for simple hot structures, and prefer well-tested library implementations.
fields.Hint: CAS retry loop; ABA when a value changes and changes back.
fields.Fact: CAS loops retry on change; ABA needs versioned pointers or safe reclamation.
fields.Source: OSTEP: Locks (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-locks.pdf)

fields.Question: A service reads a configuration map on every request (100k reads per second) and updates it once a minute. How would you synchronise access?
fields.Answer:
Best fit: copy-on-write. Keep the config in an immutable object referenced by one variable. The updater builds a complete new map and swaps the reference; readers just read the reference and use whatever version they got. Reads take no lock.

import threading

class ConfigHolder:
    def __init__(self, initial):
        self._current = dict(initial)
        self._write_lock = threading.Lock()

    def get(self):
        return self._current

    def update(self, changes):
        with self._write_lock:
            new = dict(self._current)
            new.update(changes)
            self._current = new

Why not a readers-writer lock: even read locks write to a shared counter, so at high read rates the lock's cache line becomes the bottleneck.

Caveats: readers must not mutate the returned map (wrap it, e.g. types.MappingProxyType); in Java or C++ the reference must be volatile/atomic so readers see the fully built object; old versions are reclaimed by GC here, while the kernel's RCU solves the same problem with grace periods.
fields.Hint: Copy-on-write with an atomic reference swap.
fields.Fact: Read-mostly data: immutable snapshots plus atomic pointer swap.
fields.Source:
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)
threading, Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html)

fields.Question: A concurrent hash map protected by one global lock is a bottleneck at 32 threads. How do you scale it, and what does each option cost?
fields.Answer:
• Lock striping: K locks, key hashes to one stripe. Operations on different stripes run in parallel. Cost: whole-map operations (size, resize, iteration) need all stripes, acquired in a fixed order.
  • Finer-grained buckets: Java's ConcurrentHashMap uses CAS for empty bins and locks individual bins otherwise, with cooperative resizing.
  • Sharding by owner: partition keys among threads so each shard has a single writer and no lock (actor or thread-per-core style); cross-shard work becomes messaging.
import threading

class StripedDict:
    def __init__(self, stripes=64):
        self.locks = [threading.Lock() for _ in range(stripes)]
        self.maps = [{} for _ in range(stripes)]

    def _index(self, key):
        return hash(key) % len(self.locks)

    def put(self, key, value):
        i = self._index(key)
        with self.locks[i]:
            self.maps[i][key] = value

    def get(self, key, default=None):
        i = self._index(key)
        with self.locks[i]:
            return self.maps[i].get(key, default)

Pitfalls: hot keys still serialise on one stripe; stripes packed in one array can false-share cache lines; size() becomes approximate or expensive. Measure first, since the real fix is sometimes reducing how often you touch shared state.
fields.Hint: Lock striping, then per-bucket CAS, then sharding by key.
fields.Fact: Scale shared maps with striping or sharding; global ops get harder.
fields.Source:
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)
What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory (https://people.freebsd.org/~lstewart/articles/cpumemory.pdf)

fields.Question: Thread A writes data = 42 and then ready = True. Thread B loops until ready is True and then reads data. In C++ or Java, without locks or atomics, B can read a stale data or loop forever. Why, and what is the fix?
fields.Answer:
Why: compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations and keep values in registers or store buffers. Without a happens-before relationship, B may see ready before data, or the compiler may hoist the ready read out of the loop and spin forever. In C++ this is a data race and undefined behaviour.

Fix: make ready an atomic with release on store and acquire on load (std::atomic with memory_order_release/acquire, Java volatile or AtomicBoolean), or protect both with the same mutex. A release store makes all prior writes visible to a thread that performs an acquire load and sees that store.

Python: the GIL hides most of this in practice, but threading.Event is the correct way to publish "data is ready" and it stays correct on free-threaded builds.

Follow-up: double-checked locking for lazy singletons is broken without this: another thread can see a non-null reference to a partially constructed object unless the field is volatile/atomic.
fields.Hint: Reordering and visibility; publish with release and read with acquire.
fields.Fact: Shared flags need atomics or locks for visibility and ordering, not just atomicity.
fields.Source:
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)
OSTEP: Concurrency: An Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf)

fields.Question: Your Python service must resize 10,000 images (CPU-heavy) and also make 10,000 HTTP calls. For each workload, would you use threads, processes or asyncio, and why?
fields.Answer:
• Image resizing (CPU-bound): processes (ProcessPoolExecutor, multiprocessing), one per core. With the GIL only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time, so threads give no speedup. Exception: libraries such as Pillow or NumPy release the GIL inside C code, so threads can help there; measure.
  • HTTP calls (I/O-bound): asyncio if your client libraries are async: thousands of concurrent requests on one thread, tiny per-task memory. Threads are fine for a few hundred concurrent calls with blocking libraries, since the GIL is released while waiting on sockets.

Tradeoffs: processes cost startup time, memory, and pickling data across boundaries; threads share memory but need locks and are limited by the GIL for CPU; asyncio needs an async stack end to end and one blocking call stalls everything.

Follow-up: free-threaded CPython (3.13t onwards) lets threads run in parallel for CPU work, which changes the CPU-bound answer once your dependencies support it.
fields.Hint: CPU-bound vs I/O-bound, and what the GIL blocks.
fields.Fact: CPU-bound: processes (or no-GIL); I/O-bound: async or threads.
fields.Source:

Coroutines and Tasks (asyncio), Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html)

fields.Question: Design the concurrency model for a server that must hold 50,000 mostly idle TCP connections (chat, websockets). Thread per connection, thread pool, or event loop?
fields.Answer:
Thread per connection: simple blocking code, but each thread has a stack (often 8 MB virtual, at least tens of KB resident), and 50k threads means heavy scheduler and memory overhead. Fine for a few thousand connections.

Event loop: non-blocking sockets registered with epoll (kqueue on BSD/macOS). One thread waits for readiness on all of them, and handles only the sockets that are ready. Cost is O(ready) per wakeup, not O(connections), and per-connection state is a small object. This is what nginx, Node.js, Redis and asyncio do.

Production shape: one event loop per core (SO_REUSEPORT or accept sharding), with a worker pool for CPU-heavy or blocking work so it does not stall the loop.

Pitfalls: any blocking call on the loop thread hurts every connection; with edge-triggered epoll you must drain the socket until EAGAIN; you need explicit backpressure when a client reads slower than you write.

Modern note: goroutines and Java virtual threads give thread-per-connection style code on top of an event-driven runtime.
fields.Hint: C10K: readiness notification with epoll and non-blocking sockets.
fields.Fact: Many idle connections: non-blocking I/O with epoll, one loop per core.
fields.Source:
The C10K problem (http://www.kegel.com/c10k.html)
epoll(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/epoll.7.html)
OSTEP: Event-based Concurrency (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-events.pdf)

fields.Question: Explain how an event loop with epoll works, and the difference between level-triggered and edge-triggered mode. What bug do people hit with edge-triggered?
fields.Answer:
1. Put every socket in non-blocking mode and register it with epoll_ctl for the events you care about (readable, writable).
  2. Call epoll_wait, which sleeps until at least one registered fd is ready, and returns only the ready ones.
  3. For each ready fd, read or write as much as possible, run the callbacks or resume the coroutines waiting on it, then loop.

Level-triggered (default): epoll_wait keeps reporting the fd as long as data is available. Forgiving: if you read only part, you get told again.

Edge-triggered (EPOLLET): you are told only when the state changes from not-ready to ready. If you read part of the data and go back to epoll_wait, you may never be woken for the rest. Fix: loop reading until read returns EAGAIN. Edge mode reduces repeated wakeups and, combined with EPOLLONESHOT or EPOLLEXCLUSIVE, helps multi-threaded loops avoid thundering herds.

Why not select/poll: they pass the whole fd set in every call and scan it, O(n) per call, and select is limited to FD_SETSIZE (usually 1024).
fields.Hint: Readiness notifications; edge fires once per change.
fields.Fact: Edge-triggered epoll means drain to EAGAIN or lose wakeups.
fields.Source:
epoll(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/epoll.7.html)
OSTEP: Event-based Concurrency (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-events.pdf)

fields.Question: Processes vs threads: when would you deliberately choose multiple processes even though threads are cheaper? Give real examples.
fields.Answer:
• Fault isolation: a crash or memory corruption in one process does not take down others. Chrome runs tabs and the renderer in separate processes; PostgreSQL uses a process per connection partly for robustness.
  • Security: separate address spaces plus OS sandboxing (seccomp, different users) limit what a compromised component can touch.
  • Runtime limits: CPython's GIL, or libraries that are not thread-safe.
  • Independent lifecycle: restart, upgrade or resource-limit one worker (cgroups) without touching the rest; pre-fork servers recycle workers to cap memory leaks.

Costs: higher memory (mitigated by copy-on-write after fork), slower creation, and communication must go through IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory) with serialisation.

Threads win when components share a lot of mutable state, need low-latency communication, or you need many thousands of concurrent units.
fields.Hint: Isolation, failure containment, security, and runtime limits.
fields.Fact: Choose processes for isolation; threads for cheap shared state.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Interlude: Process API (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-api.pdf)
