OSTEP: Concurrency: An Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf)

fields.Question: A multithreaded program calls fork() to run a child task, and the child occasionally hangs forever inside malloc or logging. Why, and what should you do instead?
fields.Answer:
Why: after fork, the child contains a copy of the whole address space but only the thread that called fork. If another thread held the malloc arena lock or a logging lock at that instant, the child inherits it locked with no owner left to release it. The first malloc in the child deadlocks.

POSIX rule: in a multithreaded process, the child may only call async-signal-safe functions until it calls exec.

Do instead:

  • fork immediately followed by exec, or better posix_spawn / subprocess, which does exactly that.
  • In Python multiprocessing, use the spawn or forkserver start method (forkserver is the default on Linux since Python 3.14; spawn is the default on macOS and Windows).
  • Fork worker processes early, before starting threads.

Follow-up: pthread_atfork handlers can reset some locks but are hard to get right and do not cover third-party code.
fields.Hint: Only the calling thread survives fork; locks held by others stay locked.
fields.Fact: Never fork a multithreaded process unless you exec right away.
fields.Source:
fork(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fork.2.html)
multiprocessing, Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html)
signal-safety(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal-safety.7.html)

fields.Question: How do you choose the size of a thread pool for a service? Give a formula and its caveats.
fields.Answer:
CPU-bound: about the number of cores (sometimes cores + 1 to cover occasional stalls). More threads just add context switches and cache thrash.

Mixed / I/O-bound: threads = cores x target utilisation x (1 + wait time / compute time) (Goetz, Java Concurrency in Practice). A task that waits 90 ms on a DB and computes 10 ms on 8 cores suggests about 8 x 10 = 80 threads.

Caveats:

  • Downstream limits dominate: 200 threads against a DB pool of 20 connections just queue on the pool.
  • Little's law (concurrency = throughput x latency) gives the concurrency you need for a target throughput.
  • In containers, count the CPU quota, not the host's cores; many runtimes misread this.
  • Measure under load and tune; the formula is a starting point.

Bound the queue too: an unbounded work queue hides overload until memory runs out.
fields.Hint: Cores for CPU-bound; scale up by wait-to-compute ratio for I/O-bound.
fields.Fact: Pool size: cores for CPU work, cores x (1 + wait/compute) for blocking work, capped by downstream limits.
fields.Source:
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)
Linux kernel docs: Control Group v2 (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)

fields.Question: A producer generates work faster than consumers can handle it, and the service's memory keeps growing until it is OOM-killed. How do you fix it?
fields.Answer:
Root cause: an unbounded queue between producer and consumer. Throughput is set by the slowest stage; the excess accumulates in memory, and latency grows with it.

Options:

  • Block the producer on a bounded queue (queue.Queue(maxsize=n)), which propagates backpressure upstream.
  • Reject or shed load when full (HTTP 503 / 429), so clients back off and retry.
  • Drop low-value items or sample (metrics, logs).
  • Scale consumers, if the bottleneck is parallelisable.

import queue

work = queue.Queue(maxsize=1000)

def submit(item):
    try:
        work.put(item, timeout=0.05)
        return True
    except queue.Full:
        return False

Tradeoffs: blocking is simple but can stall upstream threads that also serve other work; shedding keeps latency bounded but needs client retries with jitter; queue size should reflect acceptable latency (queue length / service rate = waiting time).

Async equivalents: asyncio.Queue(maxsize), and await writer.drain() for sockets.
fields.Hint: Backpressure: bound the queue and pick an overload policy.
fields.Fact: Every queue between stages must be bounded, with an explicit overload policy.
fields.Source:
queue, Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/queue.html)
Coroutines and Tasks (asyncio), Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html)

fields.Question: How are goroutines (or Java virtual threads) different from OS threads, and why can you run a million of them?
fields.Answer:
• OS thread: scheduled by the kernel, fixed stack reserved up front (often 8 MB virtual on Linux), creation and switches go through the kernel, microseconds each.
  • Goroutine / virtual thread: scheduled by the language runtime onto a small pool of OS threads (M:N). Stacks start tiny (2 KB in Go) and grow as needed. Switching is a user-space operation, roughly hundreds of nanoseconds.
  • Blocking: when a goroutine does network I/O, the runtime parks it and uses epoll/kqueue under the hood, so the OS thread keeps running others. Blocking syscalls that cannot be made async cause the runtime to hand the OS thread off and start another.

Tradeoffs: you keep simple blocking-style code with event-loop scalability, but the runtime's scheduler is another layer to understand; CPU-heavy goroutines still need real cores; Java virtual threads historically pinned their carrier thread inside synchronized blocks (fixed in JDK 24).

Async/await comparison: async makes suspension points explicit in the code, while green threads hide them; both are cooperative at the I/O boundary.
fields.Hint: M:N scheduling, small growable stacks, runtime-managed blocking.
fields.Fact: Green threads: runtime-scheduled, tiny growable stacks, parked on I/O.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Concurrency: An Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf)
OSTEP: Event-based Concurrency (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-events.pdf)

fields.Question: Explain virtual memory and page faults to a teammate who is debugging a performance problem. What actually happens on a memory access, and which faults are cheap vs expensive?
fields.Answer:
1. Every process sees its own virtual address space. The CPU translates virtual pages (usually 4 KB) to physical frames using page tables the kernel maintains.
  2. The TLB caches recent translations. A TLB hit is essentially free; a miss means a page-table walk (several memory reads).
  3. If the page-table entry is missing or not permitted, the CPU raises a page fault and the kernel decides what to do.
  • Minor fault: the data is already in RAM or can be produced without I/O, e.g. first touch of freshly allocated memory (zero-filled), a shared library page already in the page cache, or copy-on-write after fork. Costs around a microsecond or less.
  • Major fault: the data must be read from disk, e.g. a swapped-out page or a not-yet-cached page of an mmapped file. Costs milliseconds on HDD and around 100 microseconds on SSD, a thousand times worse.
  • Invalid access: segmentation fault (SIGSEGV).

Debugging: compare minflt and majflt in /proc/PID/stat or ps -o min_flt,maj_flt, perf stat -e page-faults, and vmstat si/so for swap activity. Lots of major faults means the working set does not fit in RAM.

Follow-ups: huge pages reduce TLB misses; mlock pins latency-critical memory; allocation is lazy, so malloc of 1 GB succeeds instantly and the cost shows up as minor faults on first touch.
fields.Hint: Address translation, TLB, minor vs major faults.
fields.Fact: Minor faults cost microseconds; major faults hit disk and cost thousands of times more.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Paging: Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-paging.pdf)
OSTEP: Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs) (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-tlbs.pdf)
OSTEP: Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-beyondphys.pdf)
proc(5), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc.5.html)

fields.Question: "Why is my program using so much memory?" A service shows 6 GB in top. Walk through how you investigate.
fields.Answer:
1. Pick the right metric. VSZ (virtual) includes reserved but untouched memory and is usually irrelevant. RSS counts resident pages, including shared libraries and shared memory counted in every process that maps them. PSS (from /proc/PID/smaps_rollup) splits shared pages fairly. In containers, the cgroup's memory.current also counts page cache charged to the cgroup.
  2. Break it down by mapping. pmap -x or /proc/PID/smaps: heap, anonymous mmaps (thread stacks, allocator arenas), file mappings, shared memory.
  3. Ask the runtime. Python tracemalloc or memray, JVM heap vs non-heap (NMT), Go pprof heap. Compare live objects to RSS: a big gap means fragmentation, allocator caching, or native memory outside the managed heap.
  4. Check growth over time. Steady growth under constant load means a leak or unbounded cache; a plateau means a working set or a high-water mark the allocator has not returned.

Usual suspects: unbounded caches or dicts, many threads each with big stacks or allocator arenas (glibc creates up to 8 x cores arenas on 64-bit), reading whole files instead of streaming, copies from slicing large buffers, and JVM heap sized to the host instead of the container limit.

Pitfall: free memory going down on the host is often just page cache, which the kernel reclaims on demand and is not your process's fault.
fields.Hint: First establish which number you are looking at, then attribute it.
fields.Fact: Know VSZ vs RSS vs PSS, then attribute memory by mapping and by allocator before guessing.
fields.Source:
proc(5), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc.5.html)
mallopt(3), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/mallopt.3.html)
Linux kernel docs: Control Group v2 (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)
tracemalloc, Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/tracemalloc.html)

fields.Question: A long-running Python service's memory grows by about 100 MB per hour. How do you find the leak?
fields.Answer:
1. Confirm it is the Python heap: compare tracemalloc's traced memory with RSS. If RSS grows but traced memory does not, look at C extensions or allocator fragmentation instead.
  2. Take a snapshot, let it run under load, take another, and diff by traceback.
  3. Inspect the top growers: what object type, who allocates it, who still references it (gc.get_referrers, objgraph's back-reference chains).
import tracemalloc

tracemalloc.start(25)
before = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
run_workload()
after = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
for stat in after.compare_to(before, "traceback")[:10]:
    print(stat)
    for line in stat.traceback.format():
        print(line)

Common causes: module-level dicts or lists used as caches without a bound (use functools.lru_cache(maxsize=...) or TTL caches), listeners or callbacks registered and never removed, storing exception objects (they keep traceback frames and all their locals alive), reference cycles with objects that hold native resources, and thread-local or contextvar state that is never cleared.

Production tips: tracemalloc has real overhead, so enable it on one canary instance; memray can attach and track native allocations too; as a stopgap, worker recycling (gunicorn max_requests) caps the damage while you fix it.
fields.Hint: Diff tracemalloc snapshots over time, then follow references.
fields.Fact: Diff heap snapshots under load, then follow references from the biggest growers.
fields.Source:
tracemalloc, Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/tracemalloc.html)
gc, Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/gc.html)

fields.Question: Your service frees a large data structure, Python or C, yet RSS does not go down. Is this a leak? Explain what is happening and what you can do.
fields.Answer:
Usually not a leak. free() returns memory to the allocator, not necessarily to the OS. glibc malloc serves small allocations from the heap (brk) and per-thread arenas, and can only shrink the top of the heap or whole free pages. A single live object at the top, or scattered survivors, pins those pages. Large allocations above M_MMAP_THRESHOLD (128 KB by default, adjusted dynamically) use mmap and do go back on free.

Python specifics: pymalloc manages small objects in arenas and releases an arena only when every object in it is freed; one survivor keeps it resident.

What you can do:

  • Verify it is reusable: if RSS stays flat when you redo the work, the memory is being reused, not leaked.
  • Call malloc_trim(0) (glibc) to return free pages, or tune M_TRIM_THRESHOLD / M_ARENA_MAX (MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 is a common fix for multithreaded bloat).
  • Use jemalloc or tcmalloc, which return memory more eagerly and fragment less.
  • Do huge transient work in a child process that exits.

Pitfall: reading RSS right after free and concluding a leak; the real test is growth across repeated identical workloads.
fields.Hint: Allocators keep freed memory; fragmentation pins pages.
fields.Fact: Freed memory goes back to the allocator, not the OS; RSS is a high-water mark.
fields.Source:
malloc_trim(3), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/malloc_trim.3.html)
mallopt(3), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/mallopt.3.html)
OSTEP: Free-Space Management (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-freespace.pdf)

fields.Question: A pod keeps restarting and the logs just stop. You suspect the OOM killer. How do you confirm it and what are the likely fixes?
fields.Answer:
1. Check the exit reason: Kubernetes shows OOMKilled, the process exit code is 137 (128 + SIGKILL). SIGKILL cannot be caught, which is why logs stop mid-line.
  2. Read the kernel log (dmesg or journalctl -k): it prints the victim, its RSS and whether it was a cgroup (memcg) OOM or a system-wide one.
  3. Check the cgroup v2 memory.events file: oom and oom_kill counters, and memory.max for the limit.

Why Linux kills instead of failing malloc: with the default overcommit heuristic, allocations mostly succeed and pages are committed on first touch, so the failure arrives later when memory is actually used and the kernel must reclaim or kill.

Fixes:

  • Make the runtime respect the container limit (JVM -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, GOMEMLIMIT, worker counts sized to memory).
  • Find real growth: leaks, unbounded caches, loading whole files.
  • Bound concurrency, since memory per request x concurrent requests must fit.
  • Raise the limit only once you know the steady-state working set.

Follow-up: page cache charged to the cgroup is reclaimable and usually not the reason for a kill, but dirty pages written faster than the disk can absorb can be.
fields.Hint: Exit code 137, kernel log, cgroup memory events.
fields.Fact: Exit 137 + kernel OOM log + memory.events confirm it; fix the runtime's view of the limit and the growth.
fields.Source:
Linux kernel docs: Overcommit Accounting (https://docs.kernel.org/mm/overcommit-accounting.html)
Linux kernel docs: Control Group v2 (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)
signal(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal.7.html)

fields.Question: A latency-sensitive service has random 200 ms stalls. CPU is fine. How would you check whether paging or swapping is the cause, and how would you fix it?
fields.Answer:
• Signals: vmstat 1 shows si/so (swap in/out) non-zero; the process's majflt counter in /proc/PID/stat rises during stalls; PSI in /proc/pressure/memory (or the cgroup's memory.pressure) shows time stalled on memory.
  • Typical causes: working set larger than RAM or the cgroup limit, other tenants pushing the service's pages out, rarely used code or heap pages evicted and faulted back in, mmapped data files that do not fit in the page cache.
  • Fixes: reduce the working set or give it more memory; lower swappiness or disable swap for that workload; mlock or MAP_POPULATE critical regions; preload and touch memory at startup instead of on the request path; avoid THP-related compaction stalls if khugepaged or direct compaction shows up in profiles.

Also check: GC pauses can look identical from the outside, so confirm with GC logs before blaming the kernel.

Why it is so bad: a major fault blocks the faulting thread on disk I/O; if that thread holds a lock, everything behind it waits too.
fields.Hint: Look for major faults and swap-in activity correlated with the stalls.
fields.Fact: Stalls with idle CPU: check major faults, swap activity and memory pressure stall info.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-beyondphys.pdf)
proc(5), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc.5.html)
Linux kernel docs: Control Group v2 (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)

fields.Question: Summing a 10,000 x 10,000 matrix stored row-major takes 0.1 s when you loop row by row, but 1 s or more when you loop column by column. Same number of operations. Explain.
fields.Answer:
Why: memory moves in 64-byte cache lines. Row-order traversal uses all 8 doubles in each line and the hardware prefetcher streams the next lines in ahead of time. Column order jumps 80,000 bytes per step, so each access touches a new cache line (and every 4 KB page a new TLB entry); by the time you come back for the neighbour in that line it has been evicted. You pay a DRAM round trip (about 100 ns) per element instead of per 8.

Fixes: traverse in storage order; transpose once if you need the other order; for operations that need both (matrix multiply), use loop tiling/blocking so a block fits in cache; use libraries (NumPy/BLAS) that already do this.

Interview framing: Big-O treats all memory accesses as equal; real machines do not. Locality is often a bigger constant factor than the algorithmic choice between two O(n) approaches. The same reasoning explains why arrays usually beat linked lists for iteration.

Python note: in pure Python lists of floats, object indirection dominates, so the effect is smaller; in NumPy or C it is dramatic.
fields.Hint: Cache lines, prefetching and TLB reach.
fields.Fact: Access memory in the order it is laid out; cache misses dominate equal Big-O loops.
fields.Source:
What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory (https://people.freebsd.org/~lstewart/articles/cpumemory.pdf)
OSTEP: Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs) (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-tlbs.pdf)

fields.Question: You need to process a 50 GB file of records. Compare read() with a buffer vs mmap. When is mmap the better choice, and when is it worse?
fields.Answer:
• Buffered read: explicit, predictable: you copy chunks from the page cache into your buffer. Errors come back as return codes. Sequential scans with a 64 KB to 1 MB buffer are typically as fast as mmap.
  • mmap: maps the file into your address space; pages fault in on demand from the page cache with no extra copy. Great for random access into large files, for sharing read-only data between processes, and for code that wants to treat the file as an array (indexes, databases' read paths).

mmap downsides:

  • I/O happens on page faults, so latency is invisible in the code and can stall any thread touching cold data.
  • I/O errors and a truncated file arrive as SIGBUS, not error codes.
  • On 32-bit or with very large files, address space and page-table overhead matter.
  • Writes through a shared mapping have no ordering guarantees until msync, so databases using mmap for writes have had subtle durability bugs.

Answer for the 50 GB scan: stream with buffered reads, use posix_fadvise(SEQUENTIAL) or readahead, process in chunks so memory stays O(buffer). Pick mmap when access is random or the data is read repeatedly by many processes.
fields.Hint: mmap avoids copies and gives random access, but turns I/O into page faults.
fields.Fact: Sequential scan: buffered reads; random access or shared read-only data: mmap.
fields.Source:
mmap(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mmap.2.html)
OSTEP: Paging: Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-paging.pdf)

fields.Question: Redis (or any app) forks a child to write a snapshot, and memory usage jumps and latency spikes during the snapshot. Explain the mechanism and mitigations.
fields.Answer:
Mechanism: fork does not copy memory; parent and child share pages marked copy-on-write. Every page the parent modifies while the child is still writing gets copied. A write-heavy workload can approach doubling memory. fork itself must copy the page tables, which for a 50 GB process takes tens of milliseconds during which the parent is stalled.

Huge pages make it worse: with transparent huge pages, touching one byte copies 2 MB instead of 4 KB, which is why Redis recommends disabling THP.

Mitigations:

  • Leave memory headroom for COW (and set vm.overcommit_memory=1 so fork does not fail on a big process, as Redis docs recommend).
  • Disable THP for the process.
  • Snapshot from a replica instead of the primary.
  • Use append-only logs or incremental snapshots instead of full forks.

Python cousin: in pre-fork servers, reference counting and the cyclic GC write to object headers, which defeats COW sharing; gc.freeze() before forking (Instagram's fix) keeps pages shared.
fields.Hint: Copy-on-write after fork, page-table copy cost, huge pages.
fields.Fact: fork shares pages copy-on-write; writes during the snapshot copy pages, and huge pages amplify it.
fields.Source:
fork(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fork.2.html)

fields.Question: A recursive tree traversal crashes with RecursionError (or a segfault in C) on a very deep input. Explain what limit you hit and how to fix it properly.
fields.Answer:
Limit: each call uses a stack frame. OS thread stacks are a fixed size (commonly 8 MB for the main thread on Linux, often less for other threads), and overflow hits a guard page, causing SIGSEGV. CPython adds its own recursion limit (1000 by default) to fail cleanly before the C stack overflows.

Proper fix: rewrite with an explicit stack on the heap, so depth is limited only by memory.

def depth_first(root, visit):
    stack = [root]
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        visit(node)
        stack.extend(reversed(node.children))

Workarounds and their risks: sys.setrecursionlimit alone can turn RecursionError into a hard interpreter crash; pair it with a larger thread stack (threading.stack_size before starting a worker thread) if you must. Tail calls are not optimised in Python, Java or Go.

Complexity: same O(n) time; space is O(depth) either way, but heap space is far larger than stack space.
fields.Hint: Thread stacks are fixed size; convert to an explicit stack.
fields.Fact: Deep recursion overflows a fixed stack; use an explicit heap stack.
fields.Source:
sys, Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html)
OSTEP: Paging: Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-paging.pdf)

fields.Question: Each of 8 threads increments its own counter in an array `counts[thread_id] += 1`. No locks, no sharing of values, yet it scales terribly. Why?
fields.Answer:
Why: the counters sit next to each other in the same 64-byte cache line. Caches are coherent per line, so every write by one core invalidates the line in all other cores' caches. The line ping-pongs between cores and each increment waits for coherence traffic, even though the threads never touch each other's data.

Fix: pad or align each counter to its own cache line (alignas(64) in C++, @Contended in Java, separate per-thread objects), or accumulate in a local variable and write once at the end.

How to detect: perf c2c on Linux reports cache lines with heavy cross-core contention; throughput dropping as you add threads with no locks in sight is the classic symptom.

Python note: CPython with the GIL will not show this, because the bottleneck is elsewhere; it bites in C, C++, Rust, Java and Go.
fields.Hint: False sharing on one cache line.
fields.Fact: Independent data on one cache line still contends; pad hot per-thread data.
fields.Source: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory (https://people.freebsd.org/~lstewart/articles/cpumemory.pdf)

fields.Question: When do huge pages help performance, and why do some databases tell you to disable transparent huge pages?
fields.Answer:
Help: a TLB has a fixed number of entries. With 4 KB pages, a few thousand entries cover only a few MB; with 2 MB pages the same entries cover gigabytes. Large, randomly accessed in-memory data sets (JVM heaps, in-memory databases, ML workloads) see fewer TLB misses and page walks, often a several percent to tens of percent speedup.

Hurt:

  • Latency spikes when the kernel compacts memory to find contiguous 2 MB regions (direct compaction on the allocation path, khugepaged in the background).
  • Memory bloat: sparse access commits a full 2 MB per touched region.
  • Fork plus copy-on-write copies 2 MB per write.

Practice: set THP to madvise so only applications that ask for it get huge pages; or use explicitly reserved hugetlbfs pages for databases that support them (PostgreSQL huge_pages, Oracle). Redis and MongoDB historically recommend disabling THP.

How to tell: perf stat dTLB-load-misses, and AnonHugePages in /proc/meminfo or smaps.
fields.Hint: TLB reach vs memory bloat and compaction stalls.
fields.Fact: Huge pages extend TLB reach; THP's compaction and bloat can cost more than it saves.
fields.Source:
Linux kernel docs: Transparent Hugepage Support (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html)
OSTEP: Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs) (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-tlbs.pdf)
Diagnosing latency issues (https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/optimization/latency/)

fields.Question: What does a context switch actually cost, how would you measure how many your service is doing, and how do you reduce them?
fields.Answer:
Direct cost: enter the kernel, save registers, run the scheduler, restore the other thread's state; switching processes also switches the address space. Typically a few microseconds.

Indirect cost: the new thread finds caches, branch predictors and possibly the TLB cold, so it runs slower for a while. For short tasks this dominates.

Measure: vmstat 1 (cs column, system-wide), pidstat -w (per task: cswch/s voluntary, nvcswch/s involuntary), perf stat -e context-switches,cpu-migrations. Voluntary switches mean threads block (locks, I/O); involuntary switches mean threads are preempted because there are more runnable threads than cores.

Reduce:

  • Fewer threads than a thread-per-request model: event loops or right-sized pools.
  • Batch work so each wakeup does more (process all queued items, not one).
  • Less lock contention, since every blocked acquire is a voluntary switch.
  • Pin latency-critical threads to cores if migrations are high.

Pitfall: blaming context switches without measuring; a few thousand per second per core is normal.
fields.Hint: Direct cost is microseconds; the indirect cache and TLB cost is often bigger.
fields.Fact: Measure voluntary vs involuntary switches; cut them with fewer threads, batching and less contention.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Mechanism: Limited Direct Execution (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-mechanisms.pdf)
sched(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sched.7.html)

fields.Question: A Linux box has a load average of 40 on 8 cores, yet top shows CPU mostly idle. What is going on and how do you investigate?
fields.Answer:
Key insight: on Linux, load average counts runnable tasks plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep (state D), usually waiting on disk or NFS I/O, or on certain kernel locks. So high load with idle CPU usually means threads stuck waiting on storage, not CPU contention.

  1. ps -eo state,pid,comm,wchan | awk '$1=="D"' to list D-state tasks and the kernel function they are waiting in.
  2. iostat -x 1 for device utilisation, queue depth and await; check for a dead NFS mount or a saturated disk.
  3. cat /proc/PID/stack (root) or perf/offcputime to see where they block.
  4. Check PSI: /proc/pressure/io and /proc/pressure/cpu separate I/O stalls from CPU queueing.

Contrast: high load with high CPU and a long run queue (vmstat r column) is genuine CPU saturation.

Pitfall: load average is an exponentially damped 1/5/15-minute value and not normalised per core; compare it to core count and pair it with utilisation and saturation (the USE method).
fields.Hint: Linux load average includes tasks in uninterruptible sleep (D state).
fields.Fact: Linux load average counts D-state I/O waiters, so high load can mean storage stalls, not CPU.
fields.Source:
Linux Load Averages: Solving the Mystery (https://www.brendangregg.com/blog/2017-08-08/linux-load-averages.html)
The USE Method (https://www.brendangregg.com/usemethod.html)

fields.Question: Explain how the Linux scheduler shares CPU among runnable threads, and what nice values actually do. How would you make a batch job stop hurting a latency-sensitive service on the same machine?
fields.Answer:
Model: for normal threads, Linux aims for weighted fair sharing. CFS tracked each task's virtual runtime and ran the one that had received the least; since kernel 6.6 EEVDF picks by earliest eligible virtual deadline, which keeps fairness while giving latency-sensitive tasks shorter slices.

Nice: each nice step changes a task's weight by roughly 1.25x, so a nice 0 task competing with a nice 10 task gets around 9 times more CPU. Nice changes share, not strict priority; a niced task still runs when there is idle CPU.

Isolating the batch job:

  • Put it in its own cgroup with a low cpu.weight, or a hard cpu.max quota.
  • Use SCHED_IDLE or SCHED_BATCH for the batch threads.
  • Pin the service and the batch job to different cores (cpusets) if cache and core contention matter.
  • Also limit I/O (io.weight / io.max) and memory, since contention is rarely only CPU.

Pitfall: real-time policies (SCHED_FIFO) for the service look tempting but a busy RT thread can starve everything, including the kernel's own work, so use them only with care and limits.
fields.Hint: Weighted fair sharing (CFS, now EEVDF), nice changes weight, cgroups isolate.
fields.Fact: Linux does weighted fair sharing; nice and cgroup weights change shares, quotas cap them.
fields.Source:
Linux kernel docs: EEVDF Scheduler (https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html)
sched(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sched.7.html)
Linux kernel docs: Control Group v2 (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)

fields.Question: A service in a container with a CPU limit of 2 shows p99 latency spikes of about 100 ms, even though average CPU usage is only 50 percent of the limit. What is happening?
fields.Answer:
Mechanism: a CPU limit is enforced as a quota per period: limit 2 means 200 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period across all threads. A multithreaded app can burn the whole quota in the first 25 ms using 8 threads, then gets throttled for the remaining 75 ms. Averages look fine; individual requests stall.

Confirm: cpu.stat in the cgroup shows nr_throttled and throttled_usec rising.

Fixes:

  • Size thread pools and runtimes to the quota, not to the host core count (GOMAXPROCS, JVM ActiveProcessorCount, worker counts). Many runtimes now read the cgroup limit; check that yours does.
  • Raise or remove the CPU limit and rely on requests/weights for fairness (a common Kubernetes recommendation for latency-sensitive services).
  • Use cpu.max.burst to allow short bursts, where supported.

Key insight: limits throttle; requests (cpu.weight) only matter under contention. Mixing up the two is a classic production issue.
fields.Hint: CFS bandwidth throttling over the 100 ms period.
fields.Fact: CPU limits are quotas per 100 ms period; bursty multithreaded apps get throttled.
fields.Source:
Linux kernel docs: CFS Bandwidth Control (https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-bwc.html)
Linux kernel docs: Control Group v2 (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)

fields.Question: A Python service is pinned at 100 percent CPU in production. How do you find out what it is doing without restarting it?
fields.Answer:
1. top -H -p PID: is it one thread or many? One hot thread suggests a loop or a GIL-bound hotspot.
  2. py-spy top --pid PID for a live view, or py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid PID for a flame graph. It reads the process's memory from outside, with no code changes and low overhead. For native code, perf record -g -p PID and perf script into a flame graph.
  3. Read the flame graph: wide frames are where time goes. Look for unexpected hot paths: regex backtracking, JSON serialisation, logging, accidental O(n^2) loops, retries spinning without backoff.
  4. Check whether it is user or system time (top shows us vs sy). High system time suggests syscall storms: strace -c -p PID to count calls.

Pitfalls: profiling a different instance than the hot one; attaching debuggers that pause the process in production; profilers needing ptrace permission (CAP_SYS_PTRACE in containers).

Follow-up: if CPU is high in GC (JVM, Go) the fix is allocation rate, not the code that appears hottest.
fields.Hint: Sample stacks from outside the process and build a flame graph.
fields.Fact: Sample stacks externally (py-spy, perf) and read the flame graph before guessing.
fields.Source:
py-spy: Sampling profiler for Python programs (https://github.com/benfred/py-spy)
Flame Graphs (https://www.brendangregg.com/flamegraphs.html)
strace(1), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/strace.1.html)

fields.Question: A program writes a 1 GB log one small record at a time with os.write per record and is very slow. Explain why and how to fix it.
fields.Answer:
Why: each os.write is a syscall: switch to kernel mode, validate arguments, copy into the page cache, return. That fixed cost (hundreds of nanoseconds to microseconds, more with security mitigations) dominates when each write is 50 bytes. Ten million writes means seconds of pure overhead.

Fix: buffer in user space and write large chunks. Python's open() returns a buffered writer (8 KB default, configurable); in C use stdio or your own buffer; for many separate buffers use writev to send them in one call.

with open("out.log", "w", buffering=1 << 20) as f:
    for record in records:
        f.write(record)

Tradeoffs: buffered data is lost if the process crashes before a flush, so flush at sensible points (per batch, per request) and fsync only where durability matters.

How to spot it: strace -c shows a huge count of small writes; high system CPU time in top.
fields.Hint: Syscall overhead per call; buffer and batch.
fields.Fact: Syscalls have fixed overhead; batch small writes into large buffers.
fields.Source:
strace(1), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/strace.1.html)
write(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/write.2.html)
OSTEP: Mechanism: Limited Direct Execution (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-mechanisms.pdf)

fields.Question: You are designing a scheduler for a job system. Compare FIFO, shortest job first and round robin for average turnaround and response time. How would you handle a mix of short interactive jobs and long batch jobs without knowing job lengths?
fields.Answer:
• FIFO: simple, but one long job ahead of many short ones creates the convoy effect and terrible average turnaround.
  • Shortest job first (or shortest remaining time first): provably minimises average turnaround when lengths are known, but needs length estimates and can starve long jobs.
  • Round robin: time slices give good response time for everyone, but worsen turnaround; slice length trades context-switch overhead against responsiveness.

Unknown lengths: multi-level feedback queue. New jobs start at high priority with short slices; a job that uses its full slice drops a level, so CPU hogs sink and interactive jobs stay on top. Periodically boost everyone back to the top to prevent starvation, and account total time used at a level so jobs cannot game it by yielding just before the slice ends.

Practical extensions: aging, per-tenant fair share, deadlines for SLAs, and admission control so the queue cannot grow without bound.
fields.Hint: SJF optimises turnaround, RR optimises response, MLFQ learns which is which.
fields.Fact: SJF for turnaround, RR for response, MLFQ when you must learn job behaviour.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Scheduling: Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched.pdf)
OSTEP: Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-mlfq.pdf)

fields.Question: When would you pin threads to specific CPU cores, and what can go wrong if you do?
fields.Answer:
• Good reasons: latency-critical loops (trading, packet processing) that must not migrate and lose cache state; thread-per-core designs where each core owns a shard; keeping noisy work off cores reserved for a service (isolcpus, cpusets); NUMA locality so a thread runs near its memory.
  • Tools: taskset, sched_setaffinity, cgroup cpusets, numactl for memory binding.

Risks:

  • If the pinned core gets busy (interrupts, another pinned process), your thread cannot move to an idle core, so latency gets worse.
  • Hyperthread siblings share a core; pinning two hot threads to siblings halves each one's throughput.
  • In containers and VMs, the core IDs you see may not map to stable physical cores.

Answer shape: pin only with evidence (high cpu-migrations, cache misses, NUMA remote access in perf), and pair pinning with moving interrupts and other work away from those cores.
fields.Hint: Affinity helps cache locality and isolation; it removes the scheduler's flexibility.
fields.Fact: Pin for locality and isolation with evidence; otherwise let the scheduler balance.
fields.Source:
sched_setaffinity(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/sched_setaffinity.2.html)
sched(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sched.7.html)

fields.Question: write() returned success. If the machine loses power one second later, is your data on disk? Explain the layers and how to make a write durable.
fields.Answer:
No, not necessarily. write copies data into the kernel's page cache and marks pages dirty. The kernel writes them back later (typically within about 30 seconds by default). A power loss before that loses the data, even though write succeeded.

  • fsync(fd): blocks until the file's data and metadata are on stable storage, including asking the device to flush its volatile write cache.
  • fdatasync(fd): same, but skips metadata not needed to read the data back (such as mtime), so often one fewer I/O.
  • O_DSYNC / O_SYNC: make every write behave like write + fdatasync / fsync.
  • O_DIRECT: bypasses the page cache but does not by itself guarantee durability; you still need fsync or O_DSYNC for the device cache.

New files: fsync the file and then fsync the parent directory, or the directory entry may not survive a crash.

Tradeoffs: fsync costs from tens of microseconds on enterprise NVMe with power-loss protection to many milliseconds on consumer drives, so durable systems batch it (group commit).

Python: f.flush() moves data from the Python buffer to the kernel; os.fsync(f.fileno()) moves it to disk. You need both.
fields.Hint: Page cache, fsync, the device cache.
fields.Fact: write reaches the page cache; only fsync (plus directory fsync for new files) makes it durable.
fields.Source:
fsync(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fsync.2.html)
write(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/write.2.html)
Ensuring data reaches disk (https://lwn.net/Articles/457667/)

fields.Question: Write a function that atomically replaces a config file, so that after a crash readers see either the complete old file or the complete new file, never a partial one.
fields.Answer:
import os, tempfile

def atomic_write(path, data: bytes):
    directory = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(path))
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=directory, prefix=".tmp-")
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "wb") as f:
            f.write(data)
            f.flush()
            os.fsync(f.fileno())
        os.replace(tmp, path)
    except BaseException:
        os.unlink(tmp)
        raise
    dir_fd = os.open(directory, os.O_RDONLY)
    try:
        os.fsync(dir_fd)
    finally:
        os.close(dir_fd)

Why each step:

  • Temp file in the same directory, because rename is only atomic within one file system.
  • fsync before rename, otherwise after a crash the rename may be persisted but the data not, leaving an empty or truncated file (a real bug that hit applications on ext4 delayed allocation).
  • rename (os.replace) atomically swaps the directory entry; concurrent readers see old or new.
  • fsync the directory so the rename itself survives a crash.

Pitfalls: writing in place with truncate + write; preserving permissions and ownership (copy them to the temp file); Windows has different rename semantics, which os.replace papers over but durability calls differ.
fields.Hint: Write temp, fsync, rename over, fsync the directory.
fields.Fact: Atomic file update = temp file + fsync + rename + fsync directory.
fields.Source:
rename(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html)
fsync(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fsync.2.html)
All File Systems Are Not Created Equal (OSDI 2014) (https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi14/technical-sessions/presentation/pillai)
os, Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html)

fields.Question: You are building an append-only write-ahead log that must not lose acknowledged writes, and it needs 50,000 writes per second on a disk where fsync takes 2 ms. How do you design the write path?
fields.Answer:
Problem: one fsync per write caps you at about 500 writes per second.

Group commit: writers append their record to an in-memory buffer and wait. A single flusher thread writes the whole batch, calls fdatasync once, then wakes every writer in that batch to acknowledge. While one fsync is in flight, the next batch accumulates. Throughput scales with batch size; added latency is at most about one fsync.

  1. Append record with length and checksum (CRC) so recovery can detect torn or partial writes at the tail.
  2. Preallocate the log file (fallocate) so appends do not change file size, letting fdatasync skip metadata.
  3. Acknowledge only after the fsync covering your record returns.
  4. On recovery, scan forward and truncate at the first record with a bad checksum.

Tradeoffs: bigger batches give throughput, smaller give latency; some systems let clients choose (acks after fsync vs after write to page cache). Replication to other machines is an alternative to local fsync for durability, as in many distributed logs.

Pitfalls: acknowledging before the fsync; trusting fsync on drives with volatile caches that lie; ignoring fsync errors (see the fsync error question).
fields.Hint: Group commit: many records per fsync.
fields.Fact: Durable throughput comes from group commit: one fsync acknowledges a whole batch.
fields.Source:
fsync(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fsync.2.html)
OSTEP: Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/file-journaling.pdf)
Ensuring data reaches disk (https://lwn.net/Articles/457667/)

fields.Question: fsync() returns EIO. Your code logs the error and calls fsync again, which succeeds. Is the data safe? What should a database do?
fields.Answer:
Not safe. On Linux, when writeback fails the kernel may mark the dirty pages clean (or drop them) and report the error once per file description. A second fsync can succeed because there is nothing left to write, even though the data never reached disk. This was the 2018 PostgreSQL fsyncgate issue.

Correct handling:

  • Treat an fsync failure on data you need as fatal for that file: do not retry and assume success.
  • Crash or stop, then recover from your own write-ahead log, which you must still have, re-applying writes from a known good point. PostgreSQL now panics on fsync failure for this reason.
  • Do not rely on errors being reported to a file descriptor that was opened after the failure; newer kernels (4.13+, errseq) improved this but you should still keep descriptors open or handle it in-process.

Broader lesson: error paths in storage stacks are poorly tested; robust systems keep enough redundancy (WAL, checksums, replicas) to recover rather than trusting a retry.
fields.Hint: No: dirty pages may have been dropped; retrying does not rewrite them.
fields.Fact: After fsync fails, the data may be gone; do not retry, recover from your log.
fields.Source:
Fsync Errors, PostgreSQL wiki (https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Fsync_Errors)
fsync(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fsync.2.html)

fields.Question: You need the 100 most frequent words in a 200 GB text file on a machine with 8 GB of RAM. Describe the approach.
fields.Answer:
1. Stream the file once. For each word, write it to partition hash(word) % P on disk, with P chosen so each partition's distinct words fit in RAM (for example P = 256). Use buffered writers per partition.
  2. Process partitions one at a time: count with a dict, keep the partition's top 100 with a heap of size 100.
  3. Merge the per-partition top-100 lists; since a word lives in exactly one partition, the global top 100 is the top 100 of the union.

Complexity: O(N) time with two passes over the data plus disk I/O for the partition files; memory O(distinct words per partition + P x buffer).

Why not sort: external merge sort works too, O(N log N), but the hash approach is linear and simpler when you only need counts.

Pitfalls: one hot word skewing a partition is fine (it is one dict entry); too many partitions means too many open files and tiny buffers; streaming line by line keeps memory constant; if approximate is acceptable, a Count-Min Sketch with a heap does it in one pass and fixed memory.

Follow-up: distributed version is a MapReduce job with the same shuffle by hash.
fields.Hint: Hash-partition to disk so each partition fits in memory, then count and merge top-k.
fields.Fact: Data bigger than RAM: hash-partition to disk, solve each partition in memory, merge.
fields.Source: heapq, Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html)

fields.Question: df says the disk is 100 percent full. You deleted a 50 GB log file, but df still shows it full. Why, and how do you fix it without a reboot?
fields.Answer:
Why: unlink removes the directory entry, not the data. The inode and blocks are freed only when the link count is zero and no process has the file open. The service writing the log still holds it open, so the space stays allocated (du will not see it, df will).

  1. Find holders: lsof +L1 lists open files with zero links, or ls -l /proc/*/fd | grep deleted.
  2. Make the process close or reopen its log: send the signal it uses for log rotation (often SIGHUP or SIGUSR1), or restart it.
  3. If you cannot restart, truncate through procfs: : > /proc/PID/fd/N frees the blocks while the process keeps writing.

Prevention: rotate logs by rename + signal to reopen, or copytruncate where the app cannot reopen; logrotate supports both.

Related interview point: the same mechanism is a feature: create a temp file, open it, unlink it immediately, and it disappears automatically when you close it or crash.
fields.Hint: An open file descriptor keeps the inode alive.
fields.Fact: Deleted but open files keep their space until the last descriptor closes.
fields.Source:
unlink(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/unlink.2.html)
proc(5), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc.5.html)

fields.Question: A service starts failing with "Too many open files" (EMFILE) after running for a few hours. How do you diagnose and fix it?
fields.Answer:
1. Check the limit: cat /proc/PID/limits (Max open files) or ulimit -n for the shell that started it. systemd and containers set their own.
  2. Count open fds over time: ls /proc/PID/fd | wc -l. Steady growth under constant load is a leak; a stable high number at the limit means the limit is too low for your concurrency.
  3. Classify them: lsof -p PID shows sockets, files, pipes. Thousands of sockets in CLOSE_WAIT means you never close connections the peer already closed.

Common leaks: files opened without with/try-finally on an error path, HTTP clients or DB connections created per request instead of pooled, subprocesses whose pipes are not closed, watchers never cancelled.

Fixes: close deterministically (context managers, try-with-resources, defer), pool connections, set O_CLOEXEC so children do not inherit fds (Python does this by default), and raise RLIMIT_NOFILE to match your design (event-loop servers legitimately need tens of thousands).

Pitfall: raising the limit to make a leak take longer to fail.
fields.Hint: File descriptor leak or limit too low; count fds over time.
fields.Fact: EMFILE: watch the fd count over time; fix the leak before raising the limit.
fields.Source:
getrlimit(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/getrlimit.2.html)
proc(5), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc.5.html)
open(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/open.2.html)

fields.Question: A static file server copies files to sockets with a read()/write() loop and saturates CPU at 5 Gbit/s. How can the OS help you serve more?
fields.Answer:
Cost of read/write: each chunk is copied from the page cache into a user buffer and back into the socket buffer: two copies and two syscalls per chunk, with the CPU touching every byte.

sendfile(out_socket, in_file, offset, count): the kernel moves data from the page cache to the socket directly, with no user-space copy and one syscall for a large range. With NIC scatter-gather support, the data is not copied by the CPU at all. nginx's sendfile on and Kafka's consumer path use this.

import os, socket

def serve_file(conn: socket.socket, path):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        conn.sendfile(f)

Limits: no user-space transformation is possible, so TLS needs kernel TLS (kTLS) to keep the zero-copy path; compression breaks it too.

Other levers: larger socket buffers, splice for pipe-to-socket, io_uring to batch submissions, and making sure files stay in the page cache.
fields.Hint: Zero copy with sendfile, plus kernel offloads.
fields.Fact: sendfile skips the user-space copy; zero copy needs the data to pass through untouched.
fields.Source:
sendfile(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/sendfile.2.html)
mmap(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mmap.2.html)

fields.Question: Implement the core of a shell that runs a two-stage pipeline like `ls -l | grep py` using fork, pipe, dup2, exec and wait.
fields.Answer:
import os

def run_pipeline(left, right):
    read_end, write_end = os.pipe()

    pid1 = os.fork()
    if pid1 == 0:
        os.dup2(write_end, 1)
        os.close(read_end)
        os.close(write_end)
        os.execvp(left[0], left)

    pid2 = os.fork()
    if pid2 == 0:
        os.dup2(read_end, 0)
        os.close(read_end)
        os.close(write_end)
        os.execvp(right[0], right)

    os.close(read_end)
    os.close(write_end)
    _, status1 = os.waitpid(pid1, 0)
    _, status2 = os.waitpid(pid2, 0)
    return os.waitstatus_to_exitcode(status2)

run_pipeline(["ls", "-l"], ["grep", "py"])

Key insight: fork duplicates file descriptors, so every process holds both pipe ends. grep sees end-of-file only when every write end is closed, so the parent and the reader child must close their copies of write_end, or grep hangs forever.

Points to mention: exec replaces the process image but keeps fds, which is how redirection works; the parent must wait to reap children (or they become zombies); the shell reports the last command's status; if exec fails the child must _exit, not fall back into the parent's code.

Follow-ups: n-stage pipelines (n-1 pipes, close everything in every child), SIGPIPE when the reader exits early, process groups and job control for Ctrl-C.
fields.Hint: Pipe before fork, dup2 onto stdin/stdout, close every unused end.
fields.Fact: Pipelines work because fds survive fork and exec; close unused pipe ends or readers never see EOF.
fields.Source:

fields.Question: ps shows hundreds of processes in state Z (defunct) under your service. What are they, why are they there, and how do you fix it?
fields.Answer:
What: zombies are children that have exited, but whose parent has not yet called wait to collect the exit status. They hold no memory, only a process-table entry and PID. Too many exhaust PIDs and fork starts failing.

Causes: the parent spawns subprocesses and never waits (Python subprocess.Popen without wait/communicate); a parent that is itself hung; in containers, your app runs as PID 1 and inherits orphaned grandchildren, but does not reap them.

Fixes:

  • Always wait for children: subprocess.run, or Popen followed by wait.
  • Reap asynchronously with a SIGCHLD handler calling waitpid(-1, WNOHANG) in a loop, since one signal may represent several exits.
  • Set SIGCHLD to SIG_IGN if you never need exit statuses; the kernel then reaps automatically.
  • In containers use a minimal init as PID 1 (tini, docker run --init) that reaps and forwards signals.

Pitfall: kill -9 on a zombie does nothing, it is already dead; kill or fix the parent. Killing the parent makes init adopt and reap them.
fields.Hint: Exited children nobody has waited for.
fields.Fact: Zombies are unreaped children; the fix is in the parent (or PID 1), not the zombie.

fields.Question: Make a worker service shut down gracefully on SIGTERM: stop taking new work, finish in-flight jobs within a deadline, then exit. Sketch it and list the pitfalls.
fields.Answer:
import signal, threading

stopping = threading.Event()

def on_term(signum, frame):
    stopping.set()

signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, on_term)
signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, on_term)

def main(jobs, handle, drain_seconds=25):
    while not stopping.is_set():
        job = jobs.get(timeout=1)
        if job is not None:
            handle(job)
    jobs.stop_accepting()
    jobs.finish_in_flight(timeout=drain_seconds)

Why a flag: signal handlers interrupt arbitrary code. In C only async-signal-safe functions may run inside them (no malloc, no locks, no printf). Python runs handlers on the main thread between bytecodes, which is safer, but the handler should still just record the request.

Pitfalls:

  • Blocking calls without timeouts never notice the flag; poll with timeouts or wake them with a self-pipe.
  • Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 s default), then SIGKILL; drain must fit inside that, and readiness should fail first so traffic stops arriving.
  • Running as PID 1 in a container: signals with no handler are ignored, so SIGTERM does nothing unless you install a handler or use an init like tini.
  • Shell-form entrypoints (sh -c) may not forward the signal to your process.

Follow-up: idempotent jobs and at-least-once queues make an unclean kill recoverable, which you need anyway because SIGKILL cannot be caught.
fields.Hint: Signal handler only sets a flag; the main loop drains.
fields.Fact: Graceful shutdown: handler sets a flag, loop drains within the grace period, SIGKILL is the backstop.

fields.Question: This hangs forever on large outputs: `p = subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE); p.wait(); out = p.stdout.read()`. Why, and what is the fix?
fields.Answer:
Why: a pipe has a bounded kernel buffer (64 KB by default on Linux). When the child has written that much and nobody reads, its next write blocks. Meanwhile the parent is blocked in wait for the child to exit. Neither can proceed: a deadlock across two processes. With both stdout and stderr piped, reading one fully then the other can deadlock the same way.

Fix: read both pipes concurrently while the child runs. communicate() does this with threads or poll, then waits.

import subprocess

result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=60, check=True)
print(result.stdout)

Other options: redirect to files or DEVNULL if you do not need the output; stream with a reader thread per pipe for huge or long-running outputs; merge stderr into stdout (stderr=STDOUT) to have one pipe.

Pitfall: timeout without killing: subprocess.run kills the child on timeout, but a bare Popen.wait(timeout) does not.
fields.Hint: Pipe buffers fill; the child blocks writing while you block waiting.
fields.Fact: Never wait on a child before draining its pipes; use communicate or run.

fields.Question: Walk me through what happens, at the OS level, when you type `./server` in a shell and press Enter, until main() runs.
fields.Answer:
1. The shell parses the line and calls fork (or posix_spawn / vfork-style clone). The child gets a copy-on-write copy of the shell's address space and its file descriptors (stdin, stdout, stderr).
  2. The child calls execve("./server", argv, envp). The kernel checks permissions, reads the header (ELF magic, or #! for scripts, which execs the interpreter), discards the old address space and maps the program's segments. File descriptors without close-on-exec stay open.
  3. For dynamically linked binaries the kernel also maps the dynamic loader (ld-linux), which maps shared libraries, resolves symbols (lazily or eagerly) and runs initialisers.
  4. Execution jumps to the entry point (_start), which sets up the C runtime and calls main(argc, argv, envp).
  5. Nothing is read from disk up front: pages of code and data fault in on first access from the page cache, which is why the second run is faster.
  6. Meanwhile the shell waits for the child (or not, for &) and reports the exit status.

Good follow-ups to anticipate: why fork then exec instead of one spawn call (gives the child a chance to set up redirection and process groups), what the vDSO is for (fast clock_gettime without a syscall), and how strace -f shows this sequence.
fields.Hint: fork, execve, the loader, lazy page faults.
fields.Fact: Running a program = fork + execve + dynamic loader + demand paging.
